title: Bias, and Why a Bigger Sample Cannot Save You

steps.body:
A **biased** method misses the truth *systematically* — it leans the same way every time. Ask only people who answer the phone at noon, and you will keep landing in the same wrong place.

Collecting more data does not fix a lean. It just plants your estimate more firmly in the wrong spot: a more precise wrong answer.
What does a bigger sample fix?
explanationVariants: Sample size controls variability — how much your estimate bounces from sample to sample. Bias is where the whole pile sits, and no size moves it.
The 1936 Literary Digest poll asked 2.4 million people and still called the election wrong: its list of names skewed rich. Size is not a cure for a slanted list.

widget.prompt: An online poll on a team's fan page finds 91% support the coach. The site collects 500,000 responses. What does the huge sample buy?

options.label: Almost nothing — the respondents are fans, so the estimate is precisely wrong.
options.feedback: Right. Size shrinks the wobble, not the lean. Half a million fans still tell you only about fans.

options.label: A very accurate estimate of public opinion, because the sample is enormous.
options.feedback: Accuracy needs the sample to *represent* the population. This one over-represents fans no matter how many of them answer.

options.label: A margin of error near zero, so the result is trustworthy.
options.feedback: The margin of error would indeed be tiny — and that is the trap. It measures random wobble only, and says nothing about who was left out.

options.label: A random sample, since anyone could click.
options.feedback: "Anyone could" is not random: the people who DO click are self-selected, and they care more than average. Randomness must be imposed, not left to volunteers.

steps.body:
Three ways a sample tilts:

**Undercoverage** — some of the population can never be picked (landline-only lists).
**Nonresponse** — the picked ones who refuse differ from those who answer.
**Voluntary response** — the people who show up feel strongest.

All three change *who* is in the sample. None of them is a small-sample problem.

explanationVariants: Undercoverage leaves part of the population unreachable; nonresponse loses people who were reachable; voluntary response lets the keenest select themselves in.
Ask: were they never in the frame, did they refuse, or did they volunteer?

widget.prompt: Sort each flawed survey by how it goes wrong.

items.label: Phone poll using a landline-only list
items.feedback: Households without a landline can never be selected, so a slice of the population is outside the frame entirely.

items.label: Mailed survey; 8% mail it back
items.feedback: Everyone was reachable, but the 92% who ignored it are likely different from the 8% who bothered.

items.label: "Click here to tell us what you think!"
items.feedback: The people with the strongest feelings select themselves in, which is why online polls skew to the angry and the delighted.

items.label: Street survey done only at 10am on a weekday
items.feedback: People at work cannot be sampled at all at that hour, so a large group is outside the frame.

widget.missFeedback: Ask: could they be selected at all (coverage)? Were they selected and declined (nonresponse)? Or did they select themselves (voluntary)?
widget.successFeedback: Three different ways of ending up with the wrong people — and no sample size repairs any of them.

explanationVariants: A question that supplies a reason ("to protect children") pushes agreement, so the estimate is biased upward whatever the sample size.
Neutral wording states the proposal and stops. Any added justification, emotive word, or one-sided framing tilts the answer.

widget.prompt: Which question wording is least likely to bias the result?

options.label: "Do you support the proposed 8pm curfew for under-16s?"
options.feedback: Right — it states the proposal and stops, without supplying a reason to agree or disagree.

options.label: "Do you support an 8pm curfew to protect children from harm?"
options.feedback: It hands the respondent a reason to say yes. Attaching a justification to one side reliably inflates that side.

options.label: "Do you oppose the government's heavy-handed new curfew?"
options.feedback: "Heavy-handed" is loaded language, so the question argues before it asks.

options.label: "Most experts back a curfew. Do you agree?"
options.feedback: Citing authority inside the question pressures agreement — a form of leading the witness.

steps.body: Two ways to be wrong, and only one of them is fixable by asking more people.

widget.prompt: Estimate support across 5,000 residents. Use a representative method, push the sample size up, and repeat — watch which of the two errors the size dial actually fixes.
widget.successFeedback: Size shrinks the WOBBLE — the estimates cluster tighter every time you raise it. It never moves the LEAN, because a method that excludes part of the population excludes it just as thoroughly at 400 as at 20. Two different errors, and only one dial.
widget.methodFeedback: This method tilts systematically. Raising the size now makes a precise estimate of the wrong number — which is exactly how a 2.4-million-ballot poll called the 1936 election wrong.
widget.sizeFeedback: Right method, but too few people to see the wobble shrink. Raise it and watch the spread of repeated estimates close in.
widget.drawsFeedback: One sample cannot show variability. Repeat the draw and watch the estimates scatter.

hints: Two things could be wrong: the estimate wobbles (random error), or the estimate leans (bias). Ask which one the facts point at.
The sample is huge, so the wobble is tiny — a large sample makes random error small.
But the people who returned the postcard chose to. That selection is a lean, and a lean does not shrink with n.
explanationVariants: The 400,000 responses make the random error negligible, so the wobble is not the problem. The bias is: those who mailed a postcard back are not like those who did not.
The reported ±0.2% is honest arithmetic about sampling variability and completely silent about the nonresponse that actually broke the poll.

widget.prompt: A magazine mails 10 million ballots, gets 400,000 back, and reports a candidate at 57% ± 0.2%. The candidate loses badly. What went wrong?

options.label: The respondents were not representative.
options.feedback: Right, and this is close to what happened in 1936. Precision is not accuracy, and the margin of error never sees the lean.

options.label: The national sample was too small.
options.feedback: 400,000 is enormous — the random error really is about ±0.2%. The estimate was precise; it was just aimed at the wrong crowd.

options.label: The margin was calculated incorrectly.
options.feedback: The arithmetic was likely right. It answers a question — how much does this estimate wobble? — that was not the one that mattered.

options.label: The result was ordinary sampling luck.
options.feedback: A miss of that size from a 400,000-person random sample is essentially impossible by chance. That rules luck out and points squarely at bias.

takeaways: Variability is random scatter around the truth; bias is a systematic miss. Sample size only touches the first.
Undercoverage, nonresponse, voluntary response and loaded wording all change WHO is in the sample.
A tiny margin of error on a biased poll is a precise wrong answer — the most dangerous kind.
steps.teaser: Next: a sample can be perfectly unbiased and the experiment around it can still be broken. Four parts every experiment needs — and what happens when one is missing.

concept.body: Picture a dartboard. Random error scatters the darts around the bullseye. Bias moves the whole cluster off it. Throwing more darts tightens the cluster — it never re-aims it.

explanationVariants: A tight cluster far from the bullseye is precise and biased — exactly what a huge, badly-drawn sample gives you.
Bias is about WHERE the cluster sits; variability is about HOW WIDE it is.

widget.prompt: A method gives nearly the same answer every time, but that answer is 12 points from the truth. What is going on?

options.label: Low variability, high bias.
options.feedback: Right — a tight cluster in the wrong place. More data will tighten it further and move it not at all.

options.label: High variability, low bias.
options.feedback: High variability would mean the answers jump around a lot. These barely move — they are just consistently off-target.
